video_title: Deflation Is Coming — And Gold, Bitcoin & Copper Could All Get Hit
gist: Bloomberg commodity strategist Mike argues that an inflation-to-disinflation cycle is starting: energy and refined-product spikes should mean-revert, while gold, silver, copper and Bitcoin are high-volatility 'puppets' of a richly valued US stock market and vulnerable to a 10% equity drop and 5% Treasury yields.

insights.claim: US equity market capitalization is about 2.5x GDP, the highest since 1928, so a 10% equity drop equals roughly 25% of GDP in lost wealth, which the strategist treats as the dominant driver of every other asset.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Equity drawdown is the key risk factor to hedge across macro, commodities and bonds.

insights.claim: Metals, copper, gold and crypto behave as 'puppets' of the US stock market: their correlation to the S&P 500 is high and their volatility is higher, so a 10% equity fall would likely cost about 20% on a metals position.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: The diversification benefit of metals and crypto disappears exactly when equities fall; size them as leveraged equity beta.

insights.claim: US equity market cap of roughly $82T versus roughly $40T of public debt is a 2.1x ratio, the highest since 2001; the speaker argues debt-worriers ignore the asset side, since equity market value is the world's largest real-time measurable asset.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Debt-collapse hedges (gold, Bitcoin) tie to equity valuation more than to debt itself.

insights.claim: S&P 500 earnings are up about 13-14% year over year and the speaker names the equity rally itself as the main source of inflation through the wealth effect, which keeps the Fed hawkish.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: A falling stock market is what would end Fed tightening; good earnings keep rates high.

themes.theme: Fed hikes and the bond market

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield is above 5% (the speaker cites 5.24% versus China's 1.67%), the highest in about a quarter century, and futures price roughly four more Fed hikes toward 5% over the next year.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Rates are the main headwind to every high-volatility asset.

insights.claim: The speaker thinks four more hikes is overpriced because the Fed would be tightening on an energy price spike that is usually transitory; only a crude oil collapse or an equity decline would stop it, and he expects the next big Fed move to be a series of cuts.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: The risk is that tightening lands into an equity and energy reversal, then yields fall fast.

insights.claim: Reported odds of about 70% for a Fed hike on October 28, a week before the midterms and by a chair Trump appointed to cut rates, are described as extraordinary, and the speaker sees a political incentive to bring energy prices down.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Political pressure and a hawkish Fed collide near the midterms.

insights.claim: The speaker sees the 5% 10-year yield as a 'gift': if equities fall 10-20% and the Fed stops, the 10-year could drop quickly from 5% to 3%, as inflation reverts to disinflation (he cites Edward Chancellor's 'The Price of Time' on boom-bust cycles).
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Long duration is the trade if equities crack; the biggest risk to shorting bonds is a stock market fall.

insights.claim: Rising yields are driven mainly by inflation expectations and the equity-fueled wealth effect rather than by US debt supply, in the speaker's view; most central banks worldwide are hiking into an energy shock they partly caused.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Debt-supply narratives may be misattributing the bond selloff.

insights.claim: China is the world's main disinflation source: its 10-year yield is about 1.67% amid a housing crisis and export dependence, Japan's debt-to-GDP is about 200% with a 10-year near 2%, which the speaker reads as late-stage, end-of-game conditions.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Global disinflationary pressure from China undermines the 'structural inflation' thesis.

themes.theme: Energy: crude, diesel and the Iran war

insights.claim: The Bloomberg diesel (heating oil) total-return index is up about 160% over one year, an all-time high in its history, and the speaker expects this kind of spike to revert with a roughly 40% decline possible by this time next year.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Peak-spike refined-product prices historically mean-revert; he compares it to gasoline at $4 in 2008 and then $2 by year end.

insights.claim: The speaker argues the US is now a net energy exporter and the energy price spike is unlike 2008 because the US no longer imports; US/Canada surplus is expanding, the West Hemisphere sets the global marginal price, and US shale cost of production is about $55/bbl, where crude was before the Iran strike.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Supply response and exporter status cap how long high energy prices can last.

insights.claim: Both the US (biggest producer) and China (biggest consumer, with falling crude imports and EV share around 62% of car sales) have an interest in lower oil prices, and the incumbent party faces losing the midterms and the next presidency if energy bills stay elevated.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Political incentives point toward de-escalation in the Iran war and a lower crude price.

insights.claim: US natural gas is down about 20% year to date while crude is up about 60%, and the strategist treats natgas (heat, power, fertilizer) as the key sign that the energy shock is not broad-based.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Divergence between gas and oil suggests the spike is a war premium, not structural scarcity.

insights.claim: Persian Gulf exports are said to be back to about 80% of normal, and Houthi-damaged Saudi Red Sea pipelines were repaired in weeks versus a forecast of six months, which he uses to argue supply disruptions are temporary and incentive-driven.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Markets usually overestimate the length of physical supply disruptions.

insights.claim: Chinese EVs have risen from about 10% of China's car sales in 2022 to about 62% now while total car sales are falling, and the speaker believes this technology substitution, plus BYD exports, structurally erodes oil demand.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Oil demand growth is capped by EV substitution led by China.

themes.theme: Gold and silver: peak and volatility warning

insights.claim: Gold has fallen to about $4,100/oz after trading above $5,000, and the speaker has turned from long-term bull to cautious this year since its 260-day volatility is about 2.2x the S&P 500's, which he says is the opposite of how a store of value behaves.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Gold behaving as a high-beta risk asset undermines the hedge case near term.

insights.claim: The gold-to-S&P 500 100-day correlation reached about 0.65 in August, the highest in its history during an equity uptrend, whereas it is normally zero or negative.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Gold is not diversifying equity risk right now.

insights.claim: Gold priced against the Treasury long-bond index is at a four-decade high (back to 1987), and the speaker flags it as a sell signal; the last time gold volatility was this elevated relative to equities was 2007.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Relative valuation versus bonds plus volatility signals a topping process.

insights.claim: The strategist thinks the 2025-26 gold and silver highs could stand for several years and perhaps decades, as with silver after 1980 and 2011 ($50 silver bought in 2011 is barely above water), and silver's exponential run shifted supply-demand balances and pushed it to a record versus copper and crude.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Parabolic metals moves tend to cap price for years.

insights.claim: Seeing 5% yields on 2- and 10-year Treasuries is described as the biggest hurdle to diversifying into gold, copper or Bitcoin, hence his advice not to fight the Fed with assets more volatile than the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Positive real yields raise the opportunity cost of non-yielding assets.

insights.claim: Copper trades like a leveraged S&P 500: the speaker notes it has tracked the S&P (dropping three zeros) for a decade, with almost double the volatility, and it recently hit a record near $6.6-7/lb while lagging equities since 2023.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Copper strength depends on equities, not just electrification and AI demand.

insights.claim: Hedge funds' managed-money net long positions in copper are about 25-30% of open interest; the speaker expects a copper selloff (about 20% decline) in the October volatility season and warns it is the next 'pump and dump' after Bitcoin, silver, platinum, palladium, iron ore and steel.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Crowded copper longs are vulnerable to a pullback.

insights.claim: China, the world's largest copper consumer, faces a property crisis and a 1.67% 10-year yield, which the speaker sees as the real driver of copper weakness despite electrification and AI narratives.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Chinese demand weakness is the bear case for copper.

insights.claim: The Bloomberg Industrial Metals index is up only about 12% year to date, roughly the same as the S&P 500, which he reads as more evidence metals are an equity puppet.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: No independent metals leadership.

insights.claim: Record US copper inventories are, in his view, due to one person's tariff decision concentrating stocks in the US rather than a fundamental surplus, and supply chain issues in critical minerals are temporary and solvable by innovation and incentives.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Inventory and bottleneck stories may be policy artifacts.

insights.claim: The speaker holds a prediction made in Q1 2024 that Bitcoin will fall to about $10,000, reasoning that it is an equity-dependent asset with limitless competing supply; it is now about $83k, 17% below the $100k level and down about 4% year to date versus S&P 500 up about 3%.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Bitcoin is failing its test of independence from equities.

insights.claim: Millions of cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin Cash, Bitcoin SV and Dogecoin (about $14B of trading) undercut Bitcoin's scarcity story, and the speaker expects a purge of the sector.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Scarcity argument is diluted by the sheer number of coins.

insights.claim: The speaker says the 2020 Covid period (10-year yield at 0.5%, Bitcoin under $10,000) was the classic buy-bonds-sell-for-Bitcoin signal; now with a 5% 10-year, about 10x higher, the setup has reversed. Bitcoin peaked around October 10 of last year near $126k.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Bitcoin's bull case needs low real yields.

insights.claim: Brazil now grows about 44% of the world's soybeans, roughly double 20 years ago, with US/Brazil production cost around $10/bu; soybeans are trading above cost and above-average stocks-to-use mean oversupply, so the speaker expects price declines absent a weather shock.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Pricing power in oilseeds has shifted to Brazil and prices above cost incentivize more supply.

insights.claim: About one third of the US soybean crop goes to biodiesel and one third of corn to ethanol, so grains are acting as crude oil puppets; corn near $5.23 versus about $4.50 production cost invites more planting.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Grain prices follow oil; falling diesel feeds through to ags.

insights.claim: Excess July-August rain in the Corn Belt caused nitrogen loss and reduced corn yields this year, a weather effect the speaker did not expect and calls his own forecasting miss.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Weather, not equities, is the swing variable in grains.

insights.claim: General rule: in commodities, high prices cure high prices; when people argue 'this time is different' near peaks, that typically marks the top, and only metals tend to stay elevated over time.
insights.speaker: Mike (Bloomberg commodity strategist)
insights.so_what: Fade consensus narratives at parabolic highs.
